title: What Happens If You Don't Treat an Infected Tooth
metaTitle: What Happens If You Don't Treat an Infected Tooth
metaDescription: An infected tooth will not heal on its own. Learn what happens if it is left untreated, the warning signs that need urgent care, and why early treatment helps.
excerpt: An infected tooth will not heal on its own and can worsen over time. Here is what can happen if it is left untreated, and why timely care usually prevents it.
heroImageAlt: Cross-section illustration of a tooth with infection at the root tip forming an abscess.
bodyHtml:
Ignoring an infected tooth rarely makes the problem disappear — a true tooth infection does not heal on its own, and over time it can spread, damage the surrounding bone, and in uncommon cases lead to serious illness. The reassuring side of the picture is that timely dental care usually stops this progression and often saves the tooth. This article explains what can happen if an infected tooth is left untreated, without exaggeration, so you can make an informed decision to get it checked.

Why an infected tooth will not simply heal

When bacteria reach the pulp inside a tooth — through deep decay, a crack, or an old failing restoration — the body cannot clear the infection on its own, because the blood supply to that inner tissue is limited and eventually dies. Antibiotics may temporarily calm a flare-up, but they do not remove the source of infection inside the tooth. That is why dentists treat the tooth itself, typically with a root canal to clean out the infection, or with extraction if the tooth cannot be saved.

What can happen as an infection progresses

From inflammation to abscess

Early on, an infected or dying pulp may cause toothache or sensitivity. As it advances, infection can collect at the root tip and form an abscess — a pocket of pus — which may cause throbbing pain, swelling, and tenderness. An abscess sometimes drains through a bump on the gum, which can relieve pressure and reduce pain, giving a false sense that the problem has resolved when the infection is still present.

Bone loss around the tooth

Persistent infection can erode the bone surrounding the root. This can weaken the tooth's support and complicate later treatment, which is one reason earlier care tends to be simpler than care delayed for months or years.

Losing the tooth

Left long enough, an infected tooth may become unsalvageable and need to be removed. What might have been treatable with a root canal can progress to a point where extraction is the only option, which then brings the separate question of replacing the tooth.

Spread beyond the tooth

Less commonly, infection can spread into nearby tissues, causing facial swelling that can affect the jaw, and — rarely — more serious, even dangerous, complications if it reaches areas such as the floor of the mouth or beyond. Warning signs that need urgent care include significant facial swelling, swelling that affects the eye or neck, fever, or difficulty breathing or swallowing. These are reasons to seek emergency care promptly.

The encouraging part: timely care usually prevents all this

The point of understanding these consequences is not to frighten, but to show why early treatment is worthwhile. Most infected teeth are resolved predictably when seen in good time, often saving the tooth and avoiding the complications above. If you have a persistent toothache, swelling, or a gum bump, prompt assessment is the sensible move. You can find out more about dental emergency care at Smile Dental Arts Centre if you are dealing with pain or swelling now.

Can a tooth infection go away without treatment?

A genuine infection of the tooth's pulp or root does not cure itself. Symptoms may ease temporarily, but the underlying infection remains until the tooth is treated.

Will antibiotics fix an infected tooth?

Antibiotics can help control a spreading infection as a short-term measure, but they do not remove the infection inside the tooth. Definitive treatment — root canal or extraction — addresses the source.

When is a tooth infection an emergency?

Rapidly increasing swelling, fever, swelling near the eye or neck, or trouble breathing or swallowing all call for urgent care without delay. When in doubt, it is safer to be assessed than to wait and watch.

Getting seen in time

If you suspect a tooth infection, having it assessed early gives the best chance of a simpler outcome. Dr. Neda Kadivar, a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience, can examine a painful or infected tooth at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham, Ontario, and recommend appropriate treatment.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
